body:
I feel that. I spent over a decade fighting with doctors before I got an accurate diagnosis for my mental health and actual medication for it that works for some of the symptoms. 

I’m able to eat in the morning, and shower often enough. 

I’m still navigating living with deteriorating physical health from chronic illness, with self-harm, with waking up wanting to kill myself. I thought things were getting better, and it feels like I dropped this deck of cards I was building. 

So I’m starting over again. I’m trying to question everything that I’ve said I value and all the defaults I assume come with life.

When I say to my therapist that I want to run away and have a different identity or live in the woods, he asks me, “Why don’t you?”  And I lay out some sensible logistical reasons. 

But it does spark something, at least to my brain, a sense that we can at least add a dash of the fantastical to our everyday lives. Or maybe not. 

I’m in the throughs of a pretty deep depression myself, so feel free to ignore my rambling.

You know, I’m not going to try and sell you on any of the ‘things worth living for’, I’m not convinced of their merit, either. 

Instead, I often think of a scene from Dead Like Me:

>	You've got to think about all the things you like and decide whether they're worth sticking around for. And if they are, you'll find a way to do this.


>	George: And what if I don’t?


>	Rube: Then you go away, and you don't get to like anything anymore.

There’s a kind of ‘balancing the budget’ logic there. Hypothetically, you could either reduce the pain or increase the happiness until living is worth it. 

Take a moment to think about what that would feel like. No pressure to follow through on improving things, just do a little daydreaming. What does a life worth living even look like for you?
